query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Reactive force field (ReaxFF) simulations can be used to optimize the alloy composition of refractory high-entropy alloys such that a dense, protective oxide scale (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3) forms during high-temperature exposure, thereby enhancing the alloy's oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with known susceptibility to oxidation at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Implement ReaxFF-guided modifications by introducing targeted anti-oxidant elements (such as Al, Cr, or Si) into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Exposing the modified and unmodified alloys to aggressive oxidation conditions at high temperatures (around 1000–1100 °C) for extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, dense, and adherent oxide layer (for instance, Al2O3, Cr2O3 or CrTaO4-based scale) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The tailored addition of anti-oxidant elements promotes the formation of a thermodynamically stable oxide scale that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thus mitigating further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a lower oxidation rate (measured as reduced weight gain) and improved mechanical and chemical stability compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified RHEA, which typically forms less protective oxide layers and shows more rapid oxidation/surface degradation at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The method's effectiveness may be limited if the modified composition introduces phase instability or if the environmental conditions exceed the formation regime of the protective oxide scales.
generation.uncertainty: While simulations predict improved oxidation resistance, the precise magnitude of enhancement in long-term, real-world high-temperature environments needs to be validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline RHEA and another set with ReaxFF-informed composition modifications incorporating targeted anti-oxidant elements. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation testing at a fixed high temperature (e.g., 1100 °C) for a prolonged period (e.g., 200 hours) in an oxygen-rich environment.
measurements: Periodic weight gain measurements to quantify the oxidation rate
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to assess the formation and integrity of the oxide layers
Mechanical property tests post-oxidation (e.g., hardness or tensile testing) to evaluate degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy modified via ReaxFF guidance does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate or does not exhibit a more continuous and protective oxide scale compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties.
